module_title: Advanced Concepts - Stagflation, Core vs. Headline, and Impact on Debtors
introduction: This advanced level decodes the complex terminology used in financial newspapers. We will understand what happens when an economy stops growing but prices keep rising, and who actually 'benefits' from inflation.

core_concepts.title: Stagflation
core_concepts.description: A combination of 'Stagnation' + 'Inflation'. It is the absolute worst-case scenario for an economy. Economic growth stalls, unemployment is extremely high, and simultaneously, inflation is very high. (Normally, a recession lowers inflation, but stagflation defies this logic).

core_concepts.title: Disinflation vs. Deflation
core_concepts.description: 1. Disinflation: A decrease in the 'rate' of inflation (e.g., inflation drops from 8% to 5%. Prices are still rising, just slower). 2. Deflation: When the inflation rate turns 'negative' (< 0%). Prices of goods are actually dropping compared to last year. This is a severe sign of economic depression (e.g., Japan's lost decades).

core_concepts.title: Headline vs. Core Inflation
core_concepts.description: 1. Headline Inflation: The total, raw inflation figure representing the entire economy. 2. Core Inflation: This is Headline Inflation MINUS highly volatile items like 'Food and Energy (Fuel)'. Because onion and petrol prices jump up and down daily, economists look at 'Core' inflation to see the true, long-term trend of the economy.

core_concepts.title: Impact of Inflation (Debtors vs. Creditors)
core_concepts.description:
Inflation acts as a massive wealth redistributor. 
- Debtors (Borrowers): They GAIN from inflation. They borrowed money when it was highly valuable and are paying it back when the currency has lost its purchasing power. 
- Creditors (Lenders): They LOSE from inflation.

important_entities.name: The Phillips Curve
important_entities.significance: Proposed by A.W. Phillips, this famous economic curve states that there is an 'inverse relationship between inflation and unemployment'. (If you want low unemployment, you must accept higher inflation). However, the phenomenon of 'Stagflation' in the 1970s completely broke and disproved this curve.

trap_alerts_and_exceptions.explanation: Never mix these up. Disinflation is often the goal of the RBI (bringing inflation down from 7% to a safe 4%). Deflation is a nightmare where consumers stop buying things because they expect prices to drop further tomorrow.

mnemonics_and_tricks.explanation: Inflation always benefits the person who took the loan (Debtor), because the real value of the money they are returning is much lower.

exam_strategy_tips: The most repeated question in State PCS and UPSC regarding this topic: 'Who benefits the most during a period of continuous inflation?' The answer is always 'Debtors' (Borrowers).
